text: very much. Thanks very much. Good evening, everyone. Mr. Chair, Councillors, as was mentioned, I'm Emily Sangster. I'm a Long-Range Planner. I'm the project lead for the Affordable Housing Strategy. With me is Kim Williston, Director of FCSS, who has been a major partner in developing the strategy, given its connection to the goals of the Social Master Plan. So the strategy has been in progress since late last summer, and we're here this evening to give an overview of the process and the draft strategy, and to provide an opportunity for questions or comments that you might have. Specifically, we'll give some background on the rationale for the strategy, our process developing it, key housing needs in Beaumont that have been identified, and the proposed strategic directions and actions before we have time for discussion. I also wanted to acknowledge at the outset Councillor Barnhart's role as Chair of the Board of the Leduc Regional Housing Foundation, another of our major partners in the strategy, and her support for this initiative and for developing affordable housing options in our region. So I'll start with a bit of background on the rationale for the strategy. It's an action item in our 2019 Municipal Development Plan, and it aligns with other directional plans and policies that we have, including the Social Master Plan and our age-friendly strategy that's in progress. It also supports direction from the Edmonton Region Growth Plan to plan for all communities in the region to develop as complete communities, which include a range of housing options to suit different household types, different life stages, and different incomes. There's also a range of research indicating that affordable housing and its capacity to help households reallocate money and time for other purposes can support individual household well-being, but also engagement in the broader community and the health of local businesses. In the strategy, I wanted to note also that we've used the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation's definition of affordable, which is housing that costs less than 30% of a household's gross income. This can mean very different things for different households, and the strategy has endeavoured to take this into account. So our process in developing the strategy has unfolded in two general stages. The first one was focused on understanding needs locally, and the second has been focused on developing a strategy that addresses those needs. We've had support throughout the process from the consulting firm Urban Matters, who have provided an advisory and a peer review role for our engagement plans and our reports, and they've also contributed their knowledge of best practices in the development of the strategy. So we started in summer 2020 with project and engagement planning and consultant hiring. Based on our meetings with our working group and public and stakeholder engagement in the fall, we developed a needs assessment that was reviewed by the working group and then formed the basis for strategy development, and that was attachment one in the package this evening. Based on the working group input, best practices guidance from Urban Matters, and some additional research, we've developed the draft strategy that was the other component of tonight's package, and was also circulated to the working group. We had a final meeting with our working group last week, incorporating key comments from them from that meeting, and any arising from our discussion this evening. The strategy is to be released for an additional round of public and industry stakeholder consultation, beginning next week for three weeks. And the intent is to consider that feedback and bring a final strategy to Council for adoption no earlier than August 2021. And if we find with our upcoming engagement that some additional consultation or some additional work is needed, we're prepared to pivot and the timeframe for Council approval into Q4 of this year. And ultimately, we look forward to continuing to work with our stakeholders, with industry partners, to put strategy into practice, because affordable housing development development is a very collaborative activity. So I'll give a quick overview of the key needs identified in our needs assessment. It found that, first of all, the majority of Beaumont households are able to find a suitable and affordable home in the private market here. We're not seeing the same broad affordability concerns as, for example, Vancouver, or large parts of southern Ontario. That said, the assessment did identify gaps in four key areas. First of all, in market affordable rental housing, especially one bedroom apartments, suitable for smaller households. Second, non-market housing or below market housing, again, especially one bedrooms, suitable for households on lower or fixed incomes, especially youth and singles and seniors. Third, access to emergency shelter and transitional housing options locally. Our working group members have advised that there's a particular need in this area for shelter that serves youth, single adults facing long-term unemployment and adults and children affected by family violence. And finally, there's a need for supportive housing options that are affordable and accessible, particularly serving seniors and people with disabilities. And so our draft strategy was developed in response to these. The vision of the strategy was developed with the working group and presented for feedback in our first round of public engagement. And it is that Beaumont is an inclusive, equitable community, offering a diversity of safe, affordable housing options that meet the needs of all residents. And so based on our needs, the strategy identifies targets that specifically address both overall affordability, as well as each of the key needs. It also identifies four strategic directions that focus on, respectively, the direct municipal role, community and industry partnerships, public engagement and education, and advocacy to senior levels of government. I won't list each action individually now, although we can certainly discuss specific actions. I'll just sort of summarize that under direction one, the actions focus on how the city processes and policies and land and financial resources might be intentionally deployed in support of the housing that's needed. Under strategic direction two, the actions focus on where administration can effectively direct its attention to close information gaps with housing sector partners and promote needed housing that way. Under strategic direction three, actions focus on ensuring that residents and administration have a common understanding of some of the needs and concerns related to housing affordability, so that those can be addressed as early in development processes as possible. And finally, under strategic direction four, the actions focus on where we can direct housing related advocacy to regional, provincial and federal governing bodies. So at our working group meeting last week, there was agreement on the general direction and generally on the actions. However, there were some notable changes proposed, and these were, first of all, that targets regarding non-market housing and emergency shelter should be revised downwards to reflect how complex it is to develop these types of housing. Second, that a recommendation should be added or revised under strategic direction one to investigate the feasibility and the impact of waiving municipal fees and taxes for eligible affordable housing developments. Third, that the recommendation regarding youth emergency shelter should be revised to account for the role of children's services in this area. And fourth, that a recommendation should be added about the need for a regional approach to emergency shelter for adults. And so these recommendations will be incorporated to the greatest extent possible before the engagement begins to ensure that public and industry stakeholders can address them in their comments.
